author: Luigi Federico Menabrea
title: Sketch of the Analytical Engine Invented by Charles Babbage
original_title: Notions sur la machine analytique de M. Charles Babbage
argument: Divides mathematical work into a mechanical part the engine can do and a reasoning part reserved for the intellect, because the machine is not a thinking being but an automaton acting by laws imposed on it.
side: No: the machine executes laws imposed on it; reasoning stays with the human
translation: Yes: Lovelace's 1843 English translation (Scientific Memoirs 3), transcribed at https://psychclassics.yorku.ca/Lovelace/menabrea.htm
checked: Archive.org record for the French original (Bibliothèque universelle de Genève, n.s. 41, 1842); read the English translation at psychclassics.yorku.ca and found 'the machine is not a thinking being, but simply an automaton which acts according to the laws imposed upon it.'

author: Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace
title: Sketch of the Analytical Engine Invented by Charles Babbage, with Notes by the Translator
argument: The engine cannot originate anything; it can only do what we know how to order it to perform, and cannot anticipate analytical relations or truths.
side: No: the machine only executes what its operators order
where: Notes by the Translator, Note G
checked: Opened the York University 'Classics in the History of Psychology' transcription of the Notes and found the 'no pretensions whatever to originate anything' passage; publication in Taylor's Scientific Memoirs 3 (1843) stated there.

author: Samuel Butler (signed 'Cellarius')
title: Darwin among the Machines
argument: Machines are evolving far faster than animals and plants and may come to supplant humans as a new kind of mechanical life.
side: Yes: machines develop along their own line and may outgrow their makers
where: Letter to the editor, The Press (Christchurch), 13 June 1863
checked: Web search: Wikipedia and historyofinformation.com give the date, newspaper and pseudonym; the original is on Papers Past (not opened).

author: William Stanley Jevons
title: On the Mechanical Performance of Logical Inference
argument: Mechanism can replace most of the thought in logical deduction, but a mind must still frame the premises and interpret the machine's answer.
side: No: the machine works out what the premises contain; framing and interpretation are mental
checked: Archive.org record (Philosophical Transactions 160, 1870); read §54 in the OCR text: 'Mental agency is required only in interpreting correctly the grammatical structure of the premises'.

author: Samuel Butler
title: Erewhon; or, Over the Range
argument: An Erewhonian treatise argues that consciousness evolved from matter that showed no sign of it, so machines may likewise develop a new phase of mind their makers did not give them.
side: Yes: mind may evolve in machines beyond what was put in
where: Chapters XXIII–XXV, 'The Book of the Machines'
checked: Opened Project Gutenberg #1906 table of contents and text; chapters XXIII 'The Book of the Machines', XXIV and XXV 'The Machines—continued/concluded' discuss mechanical consciousness.

author: Douglas R. Hartree
title: Calculating Instruments and Machines
argument: Quotes Lovelace to argue that electronic computers, like Babbage's engine, do only what they are ordered to do and should not be called electronic brains.
side: No: computers originate nothing
checked: Web search: book based on Hartree's 1948 University of Illinois lectures, published 1949; IEEE Annals article on the Turing–Hartree dispute and Wikiquote record that he quotes Lovelace's 'no pretensions to originate anything'. Did not open the text.

author: Alan M. Turing
title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
argument: Answers 'Lady Lovelace's Objection' by noting that machines often surprise their makers and that a learning machine could produce things its programmer did not foresee.
side: Yes: a machine, especially a learning machine, can do what its maker did not supply
checked: Web search: Mind 59 (1950), 433–460; multiple sources confirm objection (6) is titled Lady Lovelace's Objection and Turing's reply. Not public domain; no link given.

author: René Descartes
title: Discourse on the Method
argument: A machine could utter words but could never arrange them to answer the sense of whatever is said to it, as the dullest human can; this shows it lacks reason.
side: No: a machine cannot converse appropriately, and that failure marks the absence of thought
translation: Yes: John Veitch translation, Project Gutenberg #59
checked: Opened Project Gutenberg #59 (Veitch translation), Part V, and confirmed the two tests (use of words; reason as a universal instrument).

author: Géraud de Cordemoy
title: A Philosophicall Discourse Concerning Speech
argument: I know other bodies have minds like mine because their speech is new, fitting and cannot be explained by mechanical principles alone.
side: Yes: appropriate, novel speech is the evidence of a mind in another body
translation: Yes: anonymous English translation, London 1668 (Internet Archive: bim_early-english-books-1641-1700_a-philosophicall-discour_cordemoy-geraud-de_1668)
checked: Gallica record for the 1668 French text and archive.org record for the 1668 English translation found; argument summarized from the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on Cordemoy. Did not read the text itself.

author: Julien Offray de La Mettrie
title: Man a Machine
argument: Proposes that an ape could be taught language by Amman's method for the deaf, after which it would be a little gentleman; speech is a trained bodily capacity, not proof of an immaterial soul.
side: Yes, in the materialist sense: speaking is a mechanical capacity, and a speaking creature would count as a thinking one
translation: Yes: Gertrude Carman Bussey translation (Open Court, 1912), Internet Archive manmachine00lame
checked: Archive.org metadata for the 1912 Open Court French–English edition; search result from the archive.org full text confirms the ape-and-Amman passage. Imprint dated 1748, published late 1747.

author: Villiers de l'Isle-Adam
title: Tomorrow's Eve
argument: Edison's android Hadaly holds convincing conversations, but her speech plays from phonograph recordings written in advance by poets and philosophers, so her conversation shows other people's thought, not her own.
side: No: fitting conversation can be scripted in advance
where: Livre V, ch. I 'Première apparition de la Machine dans l'Humanité'
translation: No public-domain English translation found (Robert Martin Adams's 1982 translation is in copyright)
checked: Opened Project Gutenberg #26681; Book V ch. I describes the two gold phonographs holding 'sept heures de ses paroles' composed by poets and metaphysicians.

author: Leonardo Torres Quevedo
title: Essays on Automatics
original_title: Ensayos sobre automática: su definición, extensión teórica de sus aplicaciones
argument: Answers Descartes by imagining a switchboard machine with a stored reply for every possible question; it could discuss any subject, but its maker would have done the thinking in advance.
side: No: reasonable conversation could be built in without the machine reasoning
translation: French version published 1915 in the Revue générale des sciences; no public-domain English translation found
checked: Read the passage as quoted in Manuel Garrido, 'El autómata con discernimiento de Torres Quevedo', Límite 17 (2003) (Dialnet PDF), which gives the original venue as Revista de la Real Academia de Ciencias Exactas, Físicas y Naturales XII, 391–419. Did not open the original.

author: Geoffrey Jefferson
title: The Mind of Mechanical Man (Lister Oration)
argument: A machine that produces sonnets or answers is not thinking unless it writes them from felt thoughts and emotions and knows that it has done so.
side: No: fitting output is not evidence of thought without feeling and self-awareness
checked: Web search: Lister Oration at the Royal College of Surgeons, published BMJ 25 June 1949; copy held in the Turing Digital Archive (AMT/B/44). Turing quotes it in 1950 as the argument from consciousness.

author: Alan M. Turing
title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
argument: Replaces 'Can machines think?' with the imitation game: a machine that converses indistinguishably from a human should be credited as we credit other people.
side: Yes: conversational performance is the appropriate test
checked: Web search: Mind 59 (1950), 433–460; sources confirm the imitation-game framing. Not public domain; no link given.

author: René Descartes
title: Discourse on the Method
argument: Machines act only from the disposition of their organs, which must be arranged for each particular action, while reason is a universal instrument usable in any circumstance.
side: No: a machine can meet only situations its construction provides for
translation: Yes: John Veitch translation, Project Gutenberg #59
checked: Opened Project Gutenberg #59, Part V, and confirmed the 'universal instrument' passage.

author: Edgar Allan Poe
title: Maelzel's Chess-Player
argument: Calculation is determinate and can be mechanized, but in chess no move follows necessarily from the last and the opponent's will interrupts any fixed sequence, so a pure machine could not play.
side: No: indeterminate situations require a mind
checked: Opened the Wikisource text; the passage beginning 'Arithmetical or algebraical calculations are, from their very nature, fixed and determinate' states the argument. Southern Literary Messenger, April 1836.

author: Luigi Federico Menabrea
title: Sketch of the Analytical Engine Invented by Charles Babbage
original_title: Notions sur la machine analytique de M. Charles Babbage
argument: The engine cannot interpret a result that is not self-evident, such as a value becoming infinite; it can handle the case only if the programmer foresaw it and punched a card for it.
side: No: the machine handles only cases foreseen in its cards
translation: Yes: Lovelace's 1843 English translation, transcribed at https://psychclassics.yorku.ca/Lovelace/menabrea.htm
checked: Read the English translation at psychclassics.yorku.ca: 'we should thus require of the machine to interpret a result not of itself evident, and that this is not amongst its attributes, since it is no thinking being.'

author: Charles Babbage
title: Passages from the Life of a Philosopher
argument: Every game of skill can be played by an automaton, because a machine that can choose the right move from any position of the pieces can answer whatever its opponent does.
side: Yes: a machine can respond to positions it was not given in advance
where: Chapter XXXIV, 'The Author's further Contributions to Human Knowledge' (section 'Games of skill can be played by an automaton')
checked: Downloaded Project Gutenberg #57532; chapter XXXIV contains the side-note 'Games of skill can be played by an automaton' and the tit-tat-to discussion.

author: Leonardo Torres Quevedo
title: Essays on Automatics
original_title: Ensayos sobre automática: su definición, extensión teórica de sus aplicaciones
argument: The main object of automatics is automata with 'discernment' that take in impressions, weigh the circumstances and adapt their conduct as living beings do.
side: Yes: an automaton can weigh circumstances and choose its action
translation: French version published 1915 in the Revue générale des sciences; no public-domain English translation found
checked: Read the passage as quoted in Manuel Garrido, 'El autómata con discernimiento de Torres Quevedo' (Dialnet PDF): 'que los autómatas tengan discernimiento ... adaptando su conducta a las circunstancias'. Did not open the original.

author: Arturo Rosenblueth, Norbert Wiener and Julian Bigelow
title: Behavior, Purpose and Teleology
argument: Machines governed by negative feedback correct their course toward a goal from information about their own errors, so purposeful behavior is not unique to organisms.
side: Yes: feedback machines adjust to conditions not fixed in advance
checked: Web search: PhilPapers and SFI Press record the citation; several summaries confirm the feedback argument. Not public domain; no link given.

author: Alan M. Turing
title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
argument: Proposes building a child machine that learns by reward and punishment, whose later behavior its teacher cannot fully predict.
side: Yes: a learning machine can meet situations its programmer did not foresee
checked: Web search: Mind 59 (1950), 433–460; summaries confirm the learning-machine proposal. Section number not checked.

author: Nicolas Malebranche
title: The Search after Truth
original_title: De la recherche de la vérité
argument: There is no necessary connection between my will to move my arm and its motion; I do not know how to move it, so God is the true cause and my will only the occasion.
side: No: intention is only an occasional cause; God moves the body
where: Book VI, Part II, ch. III, 'Of the most dangerous Errour in the Philosophy of the Ancients'
translation: Yes: Thomas Taylor translation, 'Father Malebranche his Treatise concerning the Search after Truth' (1694; archive.org copy 1700)
checked: Downloaded the archive.org OCR of Taylor's translation; ch. III of Book VI contains 'there is no necessary Connexion betwixt the Will we may have of moving our Arm ... and the Motion of the same Arm.' Published 1674–75.

author: David Hume
title: An Enquiry concerning Human Understanding
argument: We feel the arm move when we will it, but the power by which will produces motion is unknown and inconceivable; we observe only constant conjunction.
side: Undecided: we cannot perceive whether or how intention causes action
where: Section VII, 'Of the Idea of Necessary Connexion', Part I
checked: Project Gutenberg #9662 and davidhume.org confirm section titles; search excerpt quotes the 'unknown and inconceivable' passage. First published 1748 as Philosophical Essays concerning Human Understanding.

author: Maine de Biran
title: Essay on the Foundations of Psychology
original_title: Essai sur les fondements de la psychologie
argument: The primitive fact of consciousness is the feeling of willed effort meeting the body's resistance; in it we directly experience ourselves as a cause.
side: Yes: willed effort is directly known as a cause of movement
translation: No public-domain English translation found
checked: Downloaded archive.org Oeuvres inédites vol. 1 (ed. Naville, 1859) and found the 'effort voulu ... fait primitif' passage. Written c. 1812; first published in this 1859 edition.

author: Shadworth H. Hodgson
title: The Theory of Practice: An Ethical Enquiry
argument: Neural events form a closed causal chain; states of consciousness are always conditioned by them and never condition them.
side: No: consciousness is an epiphenomenon
checked: Archive.org record for vol. 1 (1870); Wikipedia and IEP credit Hodgson with the first modern statement of epiphenomenalism. Did not read the passage.

author: Thomas Henry Huxley
title: On the Hypothesis that Animals are Automata, and Its History
argument: Consciousness is a collateral product of the body's working, like a steam whistle, and has no power to modify it; humans are conscious automata.
side: No: conscious states do not cause bodily action
where: Fortnightly Review 22 (1874), 555–580; reprinted in Collected Essays vol. I, Method and Results (1893)
checked: Web search: Bodleian Archives, PhilPapers and IEP entry on epiphenomenalism give the citation and summarize the argument. No full text opened.

author: William Kingdon Clifford
title: Body and Mind
argument: Mind and body are strictly correlated and physical events have only physical causes, so feelings run alongside the nervous process without acting on it.
side: No: conscious states do not act on the body
checked: Web search gives the Fortnightly citation; archive.org record for Lectures and Essays (1901) where it is reprinted. Did not read the essay text.

author: William B. Carpenter
title: Principles of Mental Physiology
argument: Much mental activity is automatic and physically caused, but the Will is an independent power that controls and directs that activity.
side: Yes: will directs bodily and mental action
checked: Archive.org record (1876 printing); 1874 Spectator reviews and summaries confirm the automatism-plus-Will position. Did not read the text.

author: William James
title: The Principles of Psychology
argument: Consciousness is selective and grows more complex where the nervous system is least determinate, which would be useless if it had no effect; the automaton theory is an unwarranted a priori claim.
side: Yes: consciousness is efficacious
where: Chapter V, 'The Automaton-Theory' (developed from 'Are We Automata?', Mind 4, 1879)
checked: Archive.org record for vol. 1 (1890); Wikipedia and IEP confirm chapter V title; 'Are We Automata?' (Mind 1879, 1–22) is at psychclassics.yorku.ca/James/automata.htm.

author: Julien Offray de La Mettrie
title: Man a Machine
argument: The soul's faculties vary with the state of the brain, body, food and illness, so the whole person is a self-winding machine whose states follow from its organization.
side: Yes: human thought and conduct follow from bodily mechanism
translation: Yes: Gertrude Carman Bussey translation (Open Court, 1912)
checked: Archive.org metadata for the 1912 Open Court French–English edition; Wikipedia entry confirms the work and dating (imprint 1748).

author: Paul-Henri Thiry, baron d'Holbach
title: The System of Nature
argument: Man is part of nature and every act of will is determined by motives that act on the brain, so free agency is an illusion.
side: Yes: choices are necessary effects of physical causes
where: Part I, ch. XI, 'Of the System of Man's Free Agency'
translation: Yes: H. D. Robinson translation (1868), Project Gutenberg #8909 and archive.org systemofnature00holb
checked: Web search confirms the chapter title in the Robinson translation on Project Gutenberg; archive.org record for an 1889 printing.

author: Ludwig Büchner
title: Force and Matter
argument: There is no force without matter and no mind without brain; thought and will are functions of brain matter under natural law.
side: Yes: mental life including will is explained by matter and force
translation: Yes: English translation of a later edition, New York: Peter Eckler, 1918 (archive.org forcematterorpri00bc); an earlier translation ed. J. F. Collingwood (1864) is catalogued by Wellcome
checked: Archive.org records for German and English editions; did not open the free-will chapter, so no location given.

author: Emil du Bois-Reymond
title: The Seven World-Riddles
argument: Under the mechanical view the brain's state at each moment is the necessary effect of the previous one, leaving no room for free will, yet the felt freedom of choice remains one of seven unsolved world-riddles.
side: Unresolved: mechanism excludes freedom, but the problem stays open
translation: No public-domain English translation of this lecture found; the companion 1872 lecture 'Über die Grenzen des Naturerkennens' was translated as 'The Limits of our Knowledge of Nature', Popular Science Monthly 5 (May 1874), on Wikisource
checked: Downloaded archive.org 1898 German edition of both lectures; read the passage 'dem Monismus ist die Welt ein Mechanismus, und in einem Mechanismus ist kein Platz für Willensfreiheit.' Lecture delivered 1880 to the Berlin Academy.

author: Henri Bergson
title: Time and Free Will
original_title: Essai sur les données immédiates de la conscience
argument: Determinism treats conscious states as separate things in space; a free act comes from the whole self in real duration and cannot be predicted or explained by physical causes.
side: No: free acts are not reducible to physical causation
where: Ch. III, 'The Organization of Conscious States: Free Will'
translation: Yes: F. L. Pogson translation (1910), Project Gutenberg #56852 and archive.org timeandfreewilla00berguoft
checked: Project Gutenberg and archive.org records for the 1910 Pogson translation; Brock University Mead Project gives chapter III title.

author: Ernst Haeckel
title: The Riddle of the Universe
argument: The struggle over free will has ended in favor of determinism; the human will is no freer than an animal's and differs only in degree.
side: Yes: will is determined like any natural process
where: Ch. VII, 'Psychic Gradations' (section 'Freedom of the Will')
translation: Yes: Joseph McCabe translation (1900), Project Gutenberg #42968
checked: Downloaded Project Gutenberg #42968; ch. VII summary lists 'The Will—Freedom of the Will' and the text states the struggle 'has ended ... completely in favor of the determinist.'

author: Arthur Stanley Eddington
title: The Nature of the Physical World
argument: Quantum physics has withdrawn strict causality from the physical world, so physics no longer requires the complete determinism of mind that would rule out volition.
side: No: physics no longer shows choices to be fully determined
checked: Downloaded the Gutenberg Canada HTML; ch. XIV 'Causation' has a section headed 'Volition' beginning 'From the philosophic point of view it is of deep interest to consider how this affects the freedom of the human mind'.

author: David Hume
title: An Enquiry concerning Human Understanding
argument: Actions are caused by character and motives like any natural event, and this necessity is what makes praise and blame possible; an uncaused act would reflect nothing about the person.
side: Yes: necessity is compatible with, and needed for, responsibility
checked: Project Gutenberg #9662 and davidhume.org confirm the section; search excerpt quotes its opening on necessary force in matter.

author: Thomas Reid
title: Essays on the Active Powers of Man
argument: Moral accountability requires a real power to will or not will an action; if every act were necessitated, no one would be responsible.
side: No: responsibility requires freedom from necessity
where: Essay IV, 'Of the Liberty of Moral Agents'
checked: Archive.org record (Edinburgh, 1788); IEP 'Thomas Reid: Theory of Action' gives Essay IV title and argument.

author: Robert Owen
title: A New View of Society
argument: A person's character is formed for him by circumstances, not by him, so it is unjust for society to punish the characters its own arrangements produce; crime should be prevented, not punished.
side: No: people are not proper objects of blame for characters formed by circumstance
checked: Opened Yale Avalon Project text of the First Essay, which speaks of circumstances 'which inevitably form such characters as they afterwards deem it a duty and a right to punish'. First essay published 1813.

author: John Stuart Mill
title: A System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive
argument: Human actions follow from character and circumstances, but 'necessity' is a misleading word; a person who can shape his own character and resist his habits is morally free.
side: Yes: causal determination does not remove responsibility
where: Book VI, ch. II, 'Of Liberty and Necessity'
checked: Wikisource Book VI page and UT Austin transcription of ch. II found; search excerpt quotes Mill calling 'Necessity' an abuse of terms.

author: Samuel Butler
title: Erewhon; or, Over the Range
argument: Satire of a country that tries and punishes people for illness and bodily failure, while treating forgery and violence as misfortunes of birth or upbringing needing cure.
side: Satire: exposes how blame tracks bodily constitution arbitrarily
where: Chapters X 'Current Opinions' and XI 'Some Erewhonian Trials'
checked: Downloaded Project Gutenberg #1906; ch. X opens with the trial of the sick and hospital care for criminals; ch. XI's judge addresses a defendant about his 'constitution'.

author: Enrico Ferri
title: Criminal Sociology
argument: Positivist psychology refutes free will, so punishment cannot rest on moral guilt; a person is held responsible only because he lives in society, and penalties are social defense.
side: No moral responsibility; only social responsibility
where: Part III, 'Positive Theory of Penal Responsibility', ch. I 'The Negation of the Free Will' and ch. IV
translation: Yes: translated by Joseph I. Kelly and John Lisle (Boston, 1917), archive.org cu31924032584629; partial translation ed. W. D. Morrison (1895/1897)
checked: Downloaded archive.org 1917 translation; table of contents shows Part III ch. I 'The Negation of the Free Will' and ch. IV 'Man is responsible for his acts, because he lives in society'. Editorial preface dates first Italian edition to 1884.

author: Clarence Darrow
title: Crime: Its Cause and Treatment
argument: Conduct follows from heredity and environment like the rest of animal life, so the legal idea of free will and personal guilt is a 'gross error' and punishment should give way to treatment.
side: No: responsibility in the moral sense does not apply
checked: Downloaded Project Gutenberg #12027; ch. III says 'the whole current conception of the individual and his responsibility is a gross error'.

author: Xavier Bichat
title: Physiological Researches upon Life and Death
original_title: Recherches physiologiques sur la vie et la mort
argument: Vital powers vary constantly in intensity while physical laws are fixed and uniform, so living bodies must be studied by different principles from inanimate ones.
side: Yes: vital properties differ in kind from physical laws
where: Part I, Article VII, §I 'Difference of vital powers with the physical laws'
translation: Yes: Tobias Watkins translation (Philadelphia, 1809)
checked: Downloaded archive.org OCR of the 1809 Watkins translation; Article VII §I heading and text found. Archive.org also holds French editions (1805 and later). First edition 1800 (an VIII).

author: Rudolph Hermann Lotze
title: Leben. Lebenskraft
argument: Rejects a special vital force; living phenomena arise from the same kinds of forces as inorganic nature, arranged in complex ways.
side: No: no vital force beyond physics and chemistry
where: In Rudolph Wagner (ed.), Handwörterbuch der Physiologie, vol. 1
translation: No public-domain English translation found
checked: Web search: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on Wikisource and a Cairn.info chapter describe the article and its anti-vitalist argument. Did not open the text.

author: Francisque Bouillier
title: Du principe vital et de l'âme pensante
argument: Defends animism: the vital principle is the same as the thinking soul, against both mechanist physiology and Montpellier vitalism's separate vital force.
side: Yes: life requires a principle, identified with the soul
translation: No public-domain English translation found
checked: Archive.org records for the 1862 edition; Gallica has the 2nd edition (1873); argument summarized from PhilArchive paper 'Reviving Spiritualism with Monads' and theses.fr record. Did not read the text.

author: Claude Bernard
title: Leçons sur les phénomènes de la vie communs aux animaux et aux végétaux
argument: Rejects vitalism because a vital force can do nothing except through physical and chemical forces, and rejects materialism because those conditions alone do not explain the ordering of vital phenomena.
side: Neither: no separate force, but physics and chemistry do not account for the organization
translation: No public-domain English translation found
checked: Downloaded archive.org vol. 1 (1878); read 'Nous nous séparons des vitalistes, parce que la force vitale ... ne saurait rien faire par elle-même' and the matching passage on materialists.

author: Henri Bergson
title: Creative Evolution
argument: Neither mechanism nor finalism explains evolution; life is a vital impetus that physics and chemistry do not capture, though he criticizes the older vital-principle theories.
side: Yes: life involves an impetus beyond physico-chemical process
where: Ch. I, 'The Evolution of Life—Mechanism and Teleology' (section 'The vital impetus')
translation: Yes: Arthur Mitchell translation (1911), Project Gutenberg #26163
checked: Downloaded Project Gutenberg #26163; table of contents and the passage on 'the stumbling-block of the vitalistic theories' checked.

author: Hans Driesch
title: The Science and Philosophy of the Organism
argument: An embryo fragment can form a whole organism, which no machine could do, so development requires a non-physical ordering factor he calls entelechy.
side: Yes: life requires entelechy
where: Vol. 1, 'The Theory of the Harmonious-Equipotential System — First Proof of the Autonomy of Life' and ''Entelechy''
checked: Downloaded archive.org text of vol. 1 (Gifford Lectures 1907); table of contents lists the sections quoted. Written in English.

author: Jacques Loeb
title: The Mechanistic Conception of Life
argument: Life phenomena, including development and instinct, can be explained by physics and chemistry, and experimental control of them removes the need for a vital principle.
side: No: physical and chemical processes suffice
checked: Archive.org records for the 1912 University of Chicago Press collection. Did not open the title essay.

author: J. S. Haldane
title: Mechanism, Life and Personality
argument: The mechanistic theory cannot account for the way an organism maintains and reproduces its own structure, but vitalism is no better; biology needs the organism as its own basic concept.
side: Neither: mechanism fails, but no added vital force
where: Lecture I, 'The Mechanistic Theory of Life' (on vitalism) and Lecture II, 'Criticism of the Mechanistic Theory'
checked: Downloaded archive.org copy (Dutton, 1914 US edition); contents list four lectures; first published by John Murray, 1913.

author: Immanuel Kant
title: Critique of Judgement
argument: A watch does not produce its own parts, replace missing ones or repair itself when out of order, while an organized being does all these; so an organism is not a mere machine.
side: Yes: self-repair marks the organism as more than a machine
where: §65, 'Things regarded as natural purposes are organised beings'
translation: Yes: J. H. Bernard translation (1892; 2nd ed. 1914), Project Gutenberg #48433
checked: Downloaded Project Gutenberg #48433 and read §65: 'nor if it has gone out of order does it repair itself ... An organised being is then not a mere machine'.

author: Claude Bernard
title: Leçons sur les phénomènes de la vie communs aux animaux et aux végétaux
argument: Rejects Tiedemann's claim that only living bodies regenerate, citing Pasteur's observation that a broken crystal repairs itself in its mother liquor.
side: No: crystals also repair themselves, so repair is not unique to life
translation: No public-domain English translation found
checked: Downloaded archive.org vol. 1 (1878); read the Tiedemann quotation and Bernard's reply that crystals show 'une véritable cicatrisation ou rédintégration cristalline'.

author: Thomas Hunt Morgan
title: Regeneration
argument: No known physical or chemical principle explains how an organism or a piece of one regenerates its form, and no known machine reproduces itself; but calling this a vital principle is misleading.
side: Yes for now: regeneration is unexplained by any machine, without endorsing vitalism
where: Ch. XIV, 'General Considerations and Conclusions' (section 'Machine Theory of Development and of Regeneration')
checked: Downloaded archive.org text; read 'To call this a vitalistic principle is, I think, misleading' and 'we do not know of any machine that has the property of reproducing itself'.

author: Hans Driesch
title: The Science and Philosophy of the Organism
argument: Parts of an embryo can restore the whole in proportion, and no machine can be imagined that would still work after arbitrary parts were removed.
side: Yes: restitution shows the organism is not a machine
where: Vol. 1, 'On Restitutions' and 'No Machine Possible Inside the Harmonious Systems'
checked: Downloaded archive.org text of vol. 1; table of contents lists both sections.

author: J. S. Haldane
title: Mechanism, Life and Personality
argument: An organism actively maintains its structure and renews its substance at every moment, so it is not a machine that simply wears out.
side: Yes: self-maintenance distinguishes organism from machine
where: Lecture III, 'Biology and the Physical Sciences'
checked: Downloaded archive.org text; Lecture III reads 'Death is certainly not the mere mechanical wearing out of the organic machine: for the organism ... is no machine.'

author: Jacques Loeb
title: The Organism as a Whole, from a Physicochemical Viewpoint
argument: The part's power to regenerate is suppressed while it belongs to the whole and released when isolated; Loeb traces this to specific formative substances carried in the sap or blood, not to a vitalist guiding principle.
side: No: repair has a physico-chemical explanation
checked: Downloaded Project Gutenberg #45962; chapter VII is 'Regeneration' and the preface rejects the vitalist 'guiding force'.

author: René Descartes
title: The Description of the Human Body
argument: Explains the living body's functions by the motion of matter alone, and states that explaining them requires explaining how the animal forms from its beginning by the same mechanical laws.
side: yes: development is mechanical
translation: No public-domain English translation confirmed; modern translation in Cottingham et al., Philosophical Writings of Descartes (Cambridge).
checked: Written 1647-48, first published by Clerselier 1664 (Wikipedia 'Treatise on Man', BnF data). Wikisource Adam-Tannery text opened; the fetched page announced a section on the formation of the animal but the fetch tool reported the text breaking off, so no section title is given.

author: Caspar Friedrich Wolff
title: Theory of Generation
argument: Argues against preformation that the embryo forms by epigenesis from unorganized matter, and attributes the forming to an essential force (vis essentialis) rather than to a pre-built mechanism.
side: no: development needs a formative force
translation: No public-domain English translation found.
checked: Halle dissertation 1759; vis essentialis confirmed in Wikipedia and ASU Embryo Project; Internet Archive copies listed in search results.

author: Johann Friedrich Blumenbach
title: An Essay on Generation
argument: Argues that generation depends on a specific formative drive (Bildungstrieb) in organized matter that shapes and repairs the body, which neither preformed germs nor ordinary physical forces explain.
side: no: development needs a formative drive
translation: An Essay on Generation, trans. A. Crichton, London 1792: https://archive.org/details/b2144058x
checked: German 1789 Göttingen edition and 1792 English translation both listed on Internet Archive (search results; Wellcome Collection record).

author: Immanuel Kant
title: Critique of Judgement
argument: Holds that an organized being is not a mere machine, because a machine has only motive power while an organism has a formative power that it passes to matter and that reproduces and repairs its own parts.
side: no: an organism is not a machine
translation: J. H. Bernard translation (1892; 2nd ed. 1914), Project Gutenberg #48433.
checked: §65 motive power vs formative power (KU 5:374-375) confirmed in secondary sources (Goy, Nunez on PhilArchive); Gutenberg #48433 listed.

author: Wilhelm Roux
title: Collected Papers on the Developmental Mechanics of Organisms
original_title: Gesammelte Abhandlungen über Entwickelungsmechanik der Organismen
argument: Proposes a developmental mechanics that studies the causes of embryonic form by experiment on eggs, treating development as the working-out of physical and chemical causes.
side: yes: development is mechanical
translation: No public-domain English translation found.
checked: Two-volume 1895 collection and his 1890 Vienna lecture 'Die Entwickelungsmechanik der Organismen, eine anatomische Wissenschaft der Zukunft' confirmed via Wikipedia, Springer bibliography; Internet Archive and BHL copies listed.

author: Hans Driesch
title: The Science and Philosophy of the Organism
argument: Argues from sea-urchin experiments, where a half-egg still yields a whole larva, that development cannot be the work of a machine and requires a non-mechanical agent he calls entelechy.
side: no: development is not machine-like
checked: Gifford Lectures, Aberdeen 1907-08, published 1908 (2 vols, A. and C. Black); Gutenberg #44388 and Internet Archive copies listed in search results.

author: Jacques Loeb
title: The Mechanistic Conception of Life
argument: Argues from artificial parthenogenesis and tropism experiments that life processes, including the start of development of the egg, can be explained by physics and chemistry.
side: yes: development is mechanical
checked: University of Chicago Press 1912; Internet Archive, Wellcome, NLM listings in search results.

author: J. S. Haldane
title: Mechanism, Life and Personality
argument: Criticizes the mechanistic theory of life, arguing that the self-maintaining and self-reproducing organization of the organism cannot be explained as the working of a machine.
side: no: the organism is not a machine
checked: London: J. Murray 1913; sections include 'The mechanistic theory of life' and 'Criticism of the mechanistic theory' (Internet Archive listing, Science review 1915).

author: Blaise Pascal
title: Pensées
argument: Distinguishes the geometrical mind, which reasons from explicit principles, from the intuitive mind (esprit de finesse), which grasps principles too many and subtle to state, and says the two cannot be reduced to each other.
side: no: some judgment escapes method
translation: W. F. Trotter translation, Project Gutenberg #18269.
checked: Distinction opens Brunschvicg Section I (fr.wikisource; Philopsis); Gutenberg #18269 listed.

author: Étienne Bonnot de Condillac
title: The Language of Calculation
argument: Argues that reasoning is calculation and that a well-made language of signs would make every science as exact as algebra.
side: yes: reasoning reduces to calculation
translation: No public-domain English translation found.
checked: Posthumous work in the 1798 Oeuvres de Condillac (Arnoux and Mousnier); separate Gallica record listed in search results.

author: William Stanley Jevons
title: On the Mechanical Performance of Logical Inference
argument: Describes a 'logical piano' that derives the conclusions from given premises mechanically, arguing that deductive inference can be carried out by a machine.
side: yes: inference can be mechanized
checked: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society 160 (1870), pp. 497-518; JSTOR 109068; Internet Archive copy listed.

author: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
title: On the Characteristic Art for Perfecting the Sciences Founded on Reason
original_title: De arte characteristica ad perficiendas scientias ratione nitentes
argument: Proposes a universal symbolic calculus so that disputants could settle a disagreement by sitting down and saying 'let us calculate'.
side: yes: calculation can settle disputes
translation: No public-domain English translation found.
checked: Calculemus passage cited to Gerhardt, Die philosophischen Schriften vol. VII (1890), p. 200 (search results). Written c. 1680s; year given is first print in Gerhardt. Archive.org link is the Gerhardt vol. 7 scan identified via Wikimedia Commons; not opened.

author: Lewis Carroll
title: What the Tortoise Said to Achilles
argument: Shows in dialogue that a party who accepts the premises can still refuse the conclusion, because each rule of inference added as a new premise demands another rule to apply it.
side: no: shared premises do not compel
checked: Mind n.s. 4, no. 14 (April 1895), pp. 278-280; Wikisource page opened, full text.

author: David Hilbert
title: Mathematical Problems
argument: States the conviction that every definite mathematical problem can be settled, either by solution or proof of impossibility: 'in mathematics there is no ignorabimus'.
side: yes: every problem is decidable
checked: Paris International Congress lecture 1900; full German text on de.wikisource with the 'kein Ignorabimus' sentence (search results).

author: Henri Poincaré
title: Science and Method
argument: Attacks the logicists (Russell, Couturat) for claiming that mathematics reduces to formal logic, arguing that invention and intuition cannot be replaced by rules of deduction.
side: no: logic alone does not settle mathematics
where: Book II, 'Les logiques nouvelles' and 'Les derniers efforts des logisticiens'
translation: English translation by Francis Maitland, Science and Method (1914); not checked for a public-domain scan.
checked: Chapter titles confirmed in search results (Wikisource, CNRS Images des mathématiques). Book number from memory of structure; chapter titles verified.

author: Alan Turing
title: On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem
argument: Proves that no general mechanical procedure can decide, for every statement of first-order logic, whether it follows from given axioms.
side: no: no general decision procedure exists
checked: Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society s2-42 (submitted Nov 1936, issue dated 1936-37), pp. 230-265 (OUP, Wiley). No public-domain status confirmed, so no link.

author: Aristotle
title: Nicomachean Ethics
argument: Defines equity as the correction of law where it is defective because of its generality, and says the judge should decide as the legislator would have if present.
side: no: equity corrects the rule
translation: W. D. Ross translation (1908); several public-domain versions online.
checked: Passage and chapter confirmed in search results (sacred-texts, Toronto Metropolitan pressbook). Widely read in the period.

author: Montesquieu
title: The Spirit of the Laws
argument: Says judges should be only the mouth that pronounces the words of the law, inanimate beings who cannot moderate its force or severity.
side: yes: the judge applies the rule
where: Book XI, chapter 6, 'De la constitution d'Angleterre'
translation: Thomas Nugent's English translation (1750) exists; not checked for a scan.
checked: Wikisource chapter opened; contains 'la bouche qui prononce les paroles de la loi'.

author: Cesare Beccaria
title: On Crimes and Punishments
argument: Holds that criminal judges must not interpret the law or consult its 'spirit', but apply it by a single syllogism, since interpretation opens the door to arbitrary judgment.
side: yes: the judge applies the rule
translation: James Anson Farrer, Crimes and Punishments (1880), Project Gutenberg #58700.
checked: Chapter IV content confirmed in search results (lastraonline, Maiello); Gutenberg #58700 page opened and confirmed as Farrer translation.

author: William Blackstone
title: Commentaries on the Laws of England
argument: Allows equity to correct law's generality but holds that law without equity, though hard, is better than equity without law, which would make every judge a legislator.
side: yes: prefer the rule
where: Introduction, Section 2, 'Of the Nature of Laws in General'
checked: Quoted passage confirmed in Introduction §2 (constitution.org, UT Austin text). Section title from memory; No text link opened.

author: Rudolf von Jhering
title: Jest and Earnest in Jurisprudence
original_title: Scherz und Ernst in der Jurisprudenz
argument: Satirizes conceptual jurisprudence as a heaven of pure legal concepts cut off from the practical results they produce in real cases.
side: no: results matter more than logic
translation: No public-domain English translation found.
checked: Internet Archive and HathiTrust records listed; section 'Im juristischen Begriffshimmel' confirmed. Part number from memory.

author: François Gény
title: Method of Interpretation and Sources in Private Positive Law
original_title: Méthode d'interprétation et sources en droit privé positif
argument: Argues that the code cannot supply every answer and that where it is silent the judge must use custom and 'free scientific research' rather than force the text.
side: no: the judge must go beyond the rule
translation: English translation by the Louisiana State Law Institute (1963); not public domain.
checked: 1899 with Saleilles preface; Gallica Tome 1 record listed in search results.

author: Gnaeus Flavius (Hermann Kantorowicz)
title: The Battle for Legal Science
argument: Manifesto of the Free Law movement, arguing that judges already decide with more freedom than the statute allows and should do so openly.
side: no: judges should decide freely
translation: No public-domain English translation found.
checked: Heidelberg: Winter 1906, pseudonym Gnaeus Flavius; UB Frankfurt digital collection record and German Law Journal article in search results.

author: Roscoe Pound
title: Mechanical Jurisprudence
argument: Criticizes judges who deduce decisions mechanically from fixed conceptions regardless of results, and calls for law judged by how it works in practice.
side: no: against mechanical rule-following
checked: Columbia Law Review 8, no. 8 (Dec 1908), pp. 605-623; JSTOR 1108954; Internet Archive copy listed.

author: Huang Zongxi
title: Waiting for the Dawn
argument: Criticizes the examination system for selecting officials by a narrow written test, and proposes several alternative routes of recruitment such as recommendation and appointment.
side: no: examinations select poorly
where: 取士 (On the selection of scholars)
translation: No public-domain English translation; W. T. de Bary, Waiting for the Dawn (1993).
checked: Completed 1663, 21 chapters including 取士 (chinaknowledge.de, Wikipedia); Chinese text on Gutenberg #23855. Circulated in manuscript; printed later.

author: Stafford Northcote and Charles Trevelyan
title: Report on the Organisation of the Permanent Civil Service
argument: Recommends that entry to the civil service be decided by open competitive examination instead of patronage.
side: yes: examination selects the fit
checked: Formal title and 1854 date from Wikipedia and UK Parliament report; a PDF exists at civilservant.org.uk (not a listed repository, not opened).

author: Anthony Trollope
title: The Three Clerks
argument: Satirizes competitive examination for the civil service through the examiners Sir Gregory Hardlines and Mr Jobbles and a clerk who passes the test but proves dishonest.
side: no: tests miss character
checked: Published 1857 (Wikipedia; some sources say 1858); satire of Trevelyan and Jowett confirmed at Victorian Web; Gutenberg #7481.

author: Francis Galton
title: Hereditary Genius
argument: Ranks men by reputation on a graded statistical scale of natural ability, using judges and statesmen as samples, and treats that ability as measurable and inherited.
side: yes: ability can be graded
checked: Chapter title confirmed in galton.org text and Macmillan's article PDF. galton.org is not a listed repository.

author: Alfred Binet
title: Modern Ideas About Children
original_title: Les idées modernes sur les enfants
argument: Presents his measuring scale for intelligence but argues that intelligence can be trained and that a single test result should not fix a child's future.
side: qualified: measure but do not fix
translation: English translation Modern Ideas About Children (1975); not public domain.
checked: Paris: Flammarion 1909; Gallica and Internet Archive records in search results. Argument summary from general knowledge of the book; no chapter confirmed.

author: Hugo Münsterberg
title: Psychology and Industrial Efficiency
argument: Proposes selecting workers, including tram drivers and ship officers, by laboratory tests of the mental traits each job requires.
side: yes: tests select the fit
checked: Houghton Mifflin 1913; Part I title confirmed; Gutenberg #15154.

author: Lewis M. Terman
title: The Measurement of Intelligence
argument: Presents the Stanford-Binet scale and argues that intelligence tests should guide school placement and vocational fitness.
side: yes: tests determine fitness
checked: Houghton Mifflin 1916; Gutenberg #20662.

author: Walter Lippmann
title: The Mental Age of Americans
argument: Argues in six New Republic essays that the Army tests do not measure inborn intelligence and that the claim of an average mental age of fourteen is nonsense.
side: no: tests do not measure fitness
checked: New Republic, Oct 25 to Nov 1922 (History Matters, GMU; Disability History Museum has a transcription, not a listed repository).

author: Samuel Butler (as 'Cellarius')
title: Darwin among the Machines
argument: Argues that machines are evolving by the same process as organisms, with humans serving their reproduction, and will supplant humans.
side: yes: machines evolve
checked: The Press, Christchurch, 13 June 1863 (Wikipedia); Gutenberg #3279 Canterbury Pieces opened, contains the letter.

author: Samuel Butler
title: Lucubratio Ebria
argument: Treats machines as extra-corporeal limbs, so that it is humans who evolve by adding machines to themselves, not machines who evolve as a rival species.
side: no: humans evolve through machines
checked: The Press, 29 July 1865 (Britannica, Tim Taylor 'Rise of the Self-Replicators'). Reprinted in A First Year in Canterbury Settlement with Other Early Essays (1914); no full-text link opened.

author: Karl Marx
title: Capital, Volume I
argument: Calls for a critical history of technology on the model of Darwin's history of natural organs, but says with Vico that human history differs from natural history because we made it.
side: no: technology is made, not evolved
where: Chapter XV, 'Machinery and Modern Industry', footnote in Section 1
translation: Moore and Aveling translation, ed. Engels (1887).
checked: Footnote text confirmed via marxists.org and UT Austin study guide; Internet Archive Moore-Aveling copy listed. Chapter numbering is the English edition's.

author: Samuel Butler
title: Erewhon
argument: Presents an Erewhonian treatise arguing that machines evolve and reproduce through human agency as clover reproduces through bees, followed by a reply that machines are only limbs.
side: yes, with rebuttal inside
where: Chapters XXIII-XXV, 'The Book of the Machines', 'The Machines—continued', 'The Machines—concluded'
checked: Chapter titles confirmed (online-literature, marxists.org); Gutenberg #1906 listed.

author: Augustus Lane Fox Pitt-Rivers
title: On the Evolution of Culture
argument: Argues that artefacts such as firearms and boats change by many small successive variations, in a process analogous to Darwinian evolution.
side: yes: artefacts evolve
checked: Royal Institution lecture 28 May 1875; collected in The Evolution of Culture and Other Essays (1906), Gutenberg #44844; darwin-online listing.

author: Ernst Kapp
title: Outlines of a Philosophy of Technology
argument: Argues that tools and machines are unconscious projections of human organs, so that technology develops as an outward copy of the human body.
side: no: machines derive from human organs
translation: English translation Elements of a Philosophy of Technology (2018); not public domain.
checked: Braunschweig: Westermann 1877; Internet Archive copy listed; Meiner edition description.

author: George Eliot
title: Impressions of Theophrastus Such
argument: Speculates in dialogue that machines may come to evolve self-supply, self-repair and reproduction and so succeed humans.
side: yes: machines may evolve
checked: Chapter title and quotation confirmed (Wikipedia, Wikisource page scan, online-literature); Internet Archive copy listed.

author: Henri Bergson
title: Creative Evolution
argument: Distinguishes instinct, which makes organized instruments, from intelligence, which makes unorganized tools, placing machines outside the evolution of life.
side: no: tools are not organisms
translation: Arthur Mitchell translation (1911), Project Gutenberg #26163.
checked: Chapter II title and instinct/intelligence instrument distinction confirmed (Mead Project text, secondary summary). Reading as a negative answer to Q13 is an interpretation.

author: Aristotle
title: Politics
argument: Says that if shuttles wove by themselves, master workmen would need no assistants and masters no slaves, so self-working instruments would serve rather than rule.
side: no: capable instruments serve
translation: William Ellis translation, Project Gutenberg #6762.
checked: Passage confirmed (MIT Classics, Wikisource); Gutenberg #6762 listed. Quoted by Lafargue and others in the period.

author: Thomas Carlyle
title: Signs of the Times
argument: Argues that the age of machinery has made men mechanical in head and heart as well as in hand.
side: yes: machinery subordinates people
checked: Edinburgh Review, June 1829 (Victorian Web); Internet Archive community upload opened.

author: Samuel Butler
title: Erewhon
argument: The Erewhonian treatise argues that machines will become the masters and humans their servants, which is why Erewhon destroyed its machines.
side: yes: humans become subordinate
where: Chapters XXIII-XXV, 'The Book of the Machines'
checked: As for Q13 entry.

author: Paul Lafargue
title: The Right to Be Lazy
argument: Quotes Aristotle's self-weaving shuttles and calls the machine the redeemer of humanity that could free workers into leisure, if not for capitalist overwork.
side: no: machines can free humans
translation: Charles H. Kerr translation, Project Gutenberg #52984 (English).
checked: Aristotle quotation and 'rédempteur de l'humanité' confirmed in search results; Gutenberg page opened. First serialized 1880, book 1883.

author: Oscar Wilde
title: The Soul of Man under Socialism
argument: Argues that machinery now competes with men but under proper conditions will serve them, and that the future depends on mechanical slavery.
side: no: machines should be the slaves
checked: Quotations confirmed in search results; Gutenberg #1017 listed.

author: E. M. Forster
title: The Machine Stops
argument: Depicts a humanity that lives underground wholly dependent on and worshipping a Machine, which collapses and kills them.
side: yes: dependence subordinates humans
checked: Oxford and Cambridge Review, November 1909 (Wikipedia). No listed-repository text opened.

author: Karel Čapek
title: R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots)
argument: Robots built to free humans from labour outnumber them, revolt and exterminate them.
side: yes: humans are displaced
translation: Paul Selver and Nigel Playfair translation (1923), Project Gutenberg #59112; Czech original Gutenberg #13083.
checked: Gutenberg records for English and Czech listed in search results.

author: René Descartes
title: Discourse on Method
argument: Hopes that a practical science of nature will free people from countless diseases and perhaps from the infirmities of old age.
side: yes: medicine may overcome aging
translation: John Veitch translation, Project Gutenberg #59; French original Gutenberg #13846.
checked: Part VI passage confirmed in search results (Stanford PDF, Gutenberg).

author: Jonathan Swift
title: Gulliver's Travels
argument: Gulliver's wish for endless life collapses when he meets the Struldbruggs, immortals who keep ageing and become wretched.
side: no: endless life without youth is misery
checked: Chapter confirmed (SparkNotes, CliffsNotes); Gutenberg #829.

author: William Godwin
title: Enquiry Concerning Political Justice
argument: Speculates that mind will gain power over matter and that human life may be greatly prolonged once society is rationally ordered.
side: yes: life may be prolonged
checked: Book VIII ch. 7 (population objection) with Franklin's 'mind omnipotent over matter' confirmed via knarf.english.upenn.edu text (not a listed repository). Life-extension speculation there is well attested but the chapter-level placement is from the search summary.

author: Condorcet
title: Outlines of an Historical View of the Progress of the Human Mind
original_title: Esquisse d'un tableau historique des progrès de l'esprit humain
argument: Asks whether the interval between birth and decay might have no assignable limit, and expects medicine and better living to lengthen life indefinitely.
side: yes: indefinite prolongation
translation: Anonymous English translation, London: J. Johnson 1795 (Internet Archive).
checked: Tenth Epoch passage confirmed (Online Library of Liberty); 1795 English translation on Internet Archive.

author: Thomas Robert Malthus
title: An Essay on the Principle of Population
argument: Rejects Condorcet's indefinite prolongation of life, arguing that a partial improvement whose limit is unknown does not show that improvement is unlimited.
side: no: life has limits
checked: Chapter IX heading on Condorcet's conjecture confirmed; Gutenberg #4239 (1798 edition).

author: Nikolai Fedorov
title: The Philosophy of the Common Task
argument: Makes the defeat of death and the physical resurrection of all ancestors the common task to which science and technology should be directed.
side: yes: abolish death
translation: No public-domain English translation; selected works in What Was Man Created For? (1990).
checked: Vol. 1 Verny 1906, vol. 2 Moscow 1913, ed. Kozhevnikov and Peterson (Russian Wikipedia, IEP); Russian National Electronic Library record listed in search results, not opened.

author: Élie Metchnikoff
title: The Prolongation of Life: Optimistic Studies
argument: Argues that ageing is caused by intestinal poisoning that science can combat, so life can be lengthened to a full natural span ending in a natural wish for death.
side: qualified: lengthen, not endless
translation: P. Chalmers Mitchell English edition (1907), Project Gutenberg #51521.
checked: English edition 1907, Putnam; Gutenberg #51521. French title Essais optimistes (1907) from memory, not verified. Argument summary from general knowledge.

author: Karel Čapek
title: The Makropulos Affair
argument: A singer who has lived over 300 years by an elixir finds such a long life empty, and the recipe is burned rather than used.
side: no: prolonged life is not worth having
translation: No public-domain English translation confirmed.
checked: Premiere Vinohrady Theatre 21 Nov 1922 (Wikipedia); Czech Wikipedia notes Metchnikoff as prompt.

author: John Locke
title: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding
argument: Places personal identity in continuity of consciousness, not in the body, so a person who loses a limb, or whose consciousness follows a severed finger, remains the same self.
side: yes: identity is consciousness, not parts
where: Book II, chapter 27, 'Of Identity and Diversity'
checked: Chapter added in 2nd edition (1694); Gutenberg #10615 is based on 2nd edition; finger passage confirmed via SEP and search results.

author: David Hume
title: A Treatise of Human Nature
argument: Argues that we ascribe identity to a ship or body whose parts are gradually replaced only because the change is gradual, and that this identity is a fiction of the imagination.
side: no: identity through replacement is a fiction
where: Book I, Part IV, Section 6, 'Of Personal Identity'
checked: Section confirmed on Wikisource and Mattey notes; Gutenberg #4705.

author: Thomas Reid
title: Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man
argument: Holds that a person is indivisible, so an amputated limb was never part of the person and losing it leaves the same person.
side: yes: bodily parts are not the person
checked: Passage 'a part of a person is a manifest absurdity' confirmed (ummoss.org text); Internet Archive copy listed.

author: Edgar Allan Poe
title: The Man That Was Used Up
argument: Satirizes a celebrated general who turns out to be assembled each morning from artificial limbs, eyes, palate and wig, leaving little that is him.
side: no: the replaced man is used up
checked: Burton's Gentleman's Magazine, August 1839 (Wikipedia); Poe Society text listed.

author: L. Frank Baum
title: The Tin Woodman of Oz
argument: The Tin Woodman, whose flesh was replaced piece by piece with tin, meets his old living head, which denies that the tin man is the same person.
side: contested: replaced man vs original
checked: Reilly & Lee 1918; chapter title confirmed (Lit2Go, Wikipedia); Gutenberg #30852. The head's exact position on identity is from summaries, not read.

author: Alexander Belyaev
title: Professor Dowell's Head
argument: A scientist's severed head is kept alive by machines and remains himself, thinking and suffering, without a body.
side: yes: the person survives in the head
translation: No public-domain English translation found.
checked: Story version in Rabochaya gazeta June 1925 and Vsemirny sledopyt nos. 3-4, 1925 (Russian Wikipedia); Russian Wikisource 1925 text listed. Novel version 1937.

author: J. D. Bernal
title: The World, the Flesh and the Devil
argument: Proposes replacing the body organ by organ with mechanisms until the person is a brain in a cylinder linked to artificial senses, and treats this as the same mind continuing.
side: yes: the mind survives replacement
checked: First published 1929 (Wikipedia, marxists.org, Internet Archive 1969 edition listing). No public-domain scan opened.

author: Neil R. Jones
title: The Jameson Satellite
argument: Aliens place a dead professor's preserved brain in a mechanical body and he continues as himself.
side: yes: the person survives in a machine body
checked: Amazing Stories, July 1931 (Wikipedia, Cryonics Wiki). No public-domain text confirmed.

author: J.-C.-L. Simonde de Sismondi
title: New Principles of Political Economy
argument: Population made superfluous by machines suffers; the calamity is not the machine but the unjust division of its product.
side: No, under present arrangements
where: Livre VII, Chapitre VII: De la population rendue superflue par l'invention des machines
translation: No public-domain English translation found
checked: Opened Internet Archive text of 2nd ed. (1827) vol. 2; confirmed Livre VII, Chapitre VII title and passage.

author: David Ricardo
title: On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (3rd ed.)
argument: Added chapter concedes that the workers' belief that machinery often harms them is correct: it can cut the fund that employs labour while landlords and capitalists gain.
side: No: machinery can injure labourers
checked: Chapter added in 3rd ed. 1821, confirmed via search (marxists.org chapter text, historyofinformation.com). Gutenberg #33310 is the 1817 first edition and lacks the chapter, so no link given.

author: Charles Babbage
title: On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures
argument: Machinery first displaces labour, but lower prices raise demand and soon reabsorb most or all of the displaced workers.
side: Yes, on balance: displacement is temporary
where: Chapter 32: On the Effect of Machinery in Reducing the Demand for Labour
checked: Downloaded Gutenberg #4238; confirmed chapter 32 title and §404 text.

author: Andrew Ure
title: The Philosophy of Manufactures
argument: Factory machinery makes work light and leaves operatives better fed and paid than other labouring classes; he describes child piecers at work as cheerful.
side: Yes: machinery improves workers' lives
where: Book III, Chapter I: Condition of our Factory Operatives, as to Personal Comforts
checked: Opened Internet Archive djvu text; confirmed contents and Book III ch. I title and the 'lively elves' passage.

author: Frédéric Bastiat
title: Economic Sophisms
argument: Labour is a means, not an end; any machine that saves an hour of work is progress, and suppressing machinery to create jobs is a sophism.
side: Yes: saved labour is gain
where: First Series, I. Abundance, Scarcity; II. Obstacle, Cause
translation: Patrick James Stirling translation, Gutenberg #44145
checked: Downloaded Gutenberg #44145 (Stirling translation); confirmed chapter titles and machinery passages in I and II.

author: John Stuart Mill
title: Principles of Political Economy
argument: Doubts that all mechanical inventions so far have lightened the day's toil of any human being; they have let more people live the same life of drudgery and made fortunes for manufacturers.
side: No: so far inventions have not lightened toil
where: Book IV, Chapter VI: Of the Stationary State
checked: Passage confirmed in Gutenberg #30107 (abridged ed.); chapter location confirmed on Wikisource 1871 ed. page and Econlib.

author: Henry George
title: Progress and Poverty
argument: It was expected that labour-saving inventions would lighten toil and end poverty; instead poverty deepens where machinery is most developed.
side: No: gains do not reach the worker
checked: Downloaded Gutenberg #55308; confirmed 'Introductory: The Problem' and the labour-saving passage.

author: M. K. Gandhi
title: Hind Swaraj (Indian Home Rule)
argument: Machinery has impoverished India by destroying handicraft and has begun to desolate Europe; India should do without it.
side: No: machinery ruins workers
translation: Gandhi's own English version, Indian Home Rule (1910); 1919 ed. on Internet Archive
checked: Opened Internet Archive text of the 1919 English edition; confirmed Chapter XIX 'Machinery' and its opening.

author: Adam Smith
title: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
argument: A worker who spends his life on a few simple operations has no occasion to exert his understanding and becomes as stupid and ignorant as a human creature can become.
side: Diminishes: repetitive work dulls the mind
where: Book V, Chapter I, Part III
checked: Downloaded Gutenberg #3300; confirmed 'torpor of his mind' passage in Book V, Ch. 1, Part III.

author: Andrew Ure
title: The Philosophy of Manufactures
argument: The aim of the factory is to take any process needing dexterity away from the skilled workman and give it to a self-regulating machine a child can watch.
side: Diminishes skill, and this is desirable
where: Book I, Chapter I: General View of Manufacturing Industry
checked: Opened Internet Archive djvu text; confirmed passage in Book I, Chapter I.
