author: Walt Whitman
title: Passage to India
argument: Celebrates the Suez Canal, the transcontinental railroad and the Atlantic cable as fulfilling God's original purpose of linking the earth, after which the poet will justify the inventors.
side: yes: engineering works carry out divine intent
checked: Internet Archive, Two Rivulets (1876) reprint; stanza on 'the first intent' and 'noble inventors' read.

author: J. B. S. Haldane
title: Daedalus, or Science and the Future
argument: Says every physical or chemical invention has been hailed as an insult to some god and every biological invention as a perversion; the inventor is always a Prometheus.
side: no: invention defies the gods rather than serving them
checked: Internet Archive text; Prometheus passage read.

author: Thomas Carlyle
title: Signs of the Times
argument: Calls the age mechanical in head and heart; men hope only in mechanism, and worship an idol of Strength instead of the Beautiful and Good.
side: yes: faith in mechanism displaces worship
checked: Internet Archive text (Edinburgh Review, June 1829); 'faith', 'worship' and 'idol' passages read.

author: Timothy Walker
title: Defence of Mechanical Philosophy
argument: Reply to Carlyle's 'Signs of the Times' defending mechanical invention as freeing people from drudgery for higher pursuits.
side: no: mechanism serves the mind, it is not a false faith
checked: Web search: North American Review 33, no. 72 (July 1831): 122–136 (JSTOR 25102907). Full text not opened; argument summarised from catalogue descriptions.

author: Matthew Arnold
title: Culture and Anarchy
argument: Says 'faith in machinery' is England's besetting danger: freedom, coal, railroads, wealth and even religious organisations are treated as ends in themselves.
side: yes: machinery is valued as if it were an end
checked: Gutenberg #4212; passage read in Chapter I.

author: Edward Carpenter
title: Civilisation: Its Cause and Cure
argument: Says locomotives, machinery and telegraphs must be reduced to subjection to the real man instead of remaining objects of 'mere fetish-worship as now'.
side: yes: machinery is currently a fetish
checked: Gutenberg #44094; passage read in Section IV.

author: Henry Adams
title: The Education of Henry Adams
argument: At the 1900 Paris Exposition Adams feels the dynamos as a moral force, as early Christians felt the Cross, and finds himself inclined to pray to one.
side: yes: the dynamo becomes an object of worship
where: Chapter XXV, "The Dynamo and the Virgin (1900)"
checked: Gutenberg #2044; Chapter XXV read. Privately printed 1907, published 1918.

author: E. M. Forster
title: The Machine Stops
argument: People consult the Book of the Machine as scripture and come to worship the Machine that serves them.
side: yes: dependence becomes worship
checked: Gutenberg #72890; 'worship the Machine' passages found.

author: Nikolai Berdyaev
title: Man and Machine
argument: Argues modern civilisation puts tools in the place of their users and that, without a spiritual reorientation, technology will destroy man as a person.
side: yes: technology usurps man's spiritual place
translation: No public-domain English translation; English translation in Technology and Language (2023)
checked: Web search: published in the émigré journal Put' (Paris), 1933; soctech.spbstu.ru English translation page.

author: Charles Babbage
title: On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures
argument: Says a country must have reached a high degree of civilization before it approaches the limit of economy in applying force to transport.
side: yes: mechanical economy advances with civilization
checked: Gutenberg #4238; §19 read. §19 falls in Chapter 1.

author: Thomas Babington Macaulay
title: Lord Bacon
argument: Judges Bacon's philosophy by its fruits: it has lengthened life, spanned rivers, annihilated distance and driven cars without horses; its law is progress.
side: yes: mechanical achievement is the mark of advancement
checked: Gutenberg #2333 (Critical and Historical Essays, vol. 2); essay dated July 1837 (Edinburgh Review); passage read.

author: Lewis Henry Morgan
title: Ancient Society
argument: Divides human history into savagery, barbarism and civilization, marking the stages largely by a sequence of inventions and discoveries.
side: yes: technical invention measures the ascent to civilization
where: Part I, "Growth of Intelligence through Inventions and Discoveries"
checked: Gutenberg #45950; Part I heading and preface read.

author: M. K. Gandhi
title: Hind Swaraj, or Indian Home Rule
argument: Argues modern civilization, whose chief symbol is machinery, is an irreligious condition; true civilization is moral conduct, and India's ancestors chose not to pursue machinery.
side: no: machinery is a mark of false civilization
where: Chapter VI, "Civilisation"; Chapter XIII, "What is True Civilisation?"
translation: Gandhi's own English translation, Indian Home Rule (1910); 1921 Madras edition on Internet Archive
checked: Internet Archive 1921 edition; table of contents and chapter text read.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
title: Nationalism
argument: Argues the West has turned society into a machine of commerce and politics whose aim is success, not goodness, eliminating moral responsibility.
side: no: mechanical organisation is not moral progress
checked: Gutenberg #40766; passage in 'Nationalism in the West' read.

author: Oswald Spengler
title: Man and Technics
argument: Treats machine technology as the expression of Western man's will to power, a stage in a culture's life that ends in decline.
side: no: machinery marks a late, declining phase
translation: C. T. Atkinson (1932); public-domain status not verified
checked: English Wikipedia summary (1931 book; will-to-power reading). Text not opened.

author: Feng Guifen
title: Protests from the Jiaobin Studio
argument: China should adopt Western mathematics, mechanics and arms while keeping Chinese ethical teaching as the foundation; the principle later summarized as Chinese learning for substance, Western learning for application.
side: yes: machinery can be adopted while keeping native ways
translation: No public-domain English translation confirmed; excerpts appear in modern source readers.
checked: Britannica entries on Feng Guifen and Jiaobinlu kangyi; Wikipedia 'Chinese Learning as Substance, Western Learning for Application' credits Feng with first proposing the idea in 1861.

author: Fukuzawa Yukichi
title: An Outline of a Theory of Civilization
original_title: 文明論之概略 (Bunmeiron no gairyaku)
argument: Japan cannot take Western technical novelties while keeping its old spirit; it must adopt the spirit of civilization, the independence of the individual and the nation, that produced them.
side: no: the machinery comes with the civilization that produced it
translation: English translation by David A. Dilworth and G. Cameron Hurst (Sophia University, 1973), not public domain.
checked: Monumenta Nipponica monograph page for the Dilworth/Hurst translation; Karolinum journal article on the 1875 text summarizing its rejection of 'Japanese spirit, Western practice'.

author: Zhang Zhidong
title: Exhortation to Learning
argument: China should keep the Confucian basis of society and take Western learning only to strengthen its material basis.
side: yes: machinery can be adopted while keeping native ways
translation: China's Only Hope: An Appeal, trans. Samuel I. Woodbridge (1900), Internet Archive.
checked: Internet Archive catalogue page for Woodbridge translation (1900); HathiTrust record for Chinese text; Wikipedia ti-yong article.

author: Yan Fu
title: Letter to the Editor of the Waijiao bao
argument: Chinese and Western learning each have their own substance and application; combining Chinese substance with Western application makes both lose their meaning.
side: no: substance and function cannot be separated
translation: No public-domain English translation found.
checked: Wikipedia 'Chinese Learning as Substance, Western Learning for Application' quotes and cites Yan Fu 1902; ResearchGate article on Yan Fu and Chinese/Western learning. Primary text not opened.

author: M. K. Gandhi
title: Hind Swaraj or Indian Home Rule
argument: Machinery is the chief sign of modern civilization and has impoverished India; India cannot take it up and remain itself.
side: no: machinery carries the civilization with it
translation: Gandhi's own English translation, Indian Home Rule (1910).
checked: Wikipedia entry for Hind Swaraj; Sevagram Ashram online text of Chapter 19 'Machinery'; Cambridge edition listing.

author: Thorstein Veblen
title: Imperial Germany and the Industrial Revolution
argument: Germany borrowed English machine technology without the English institutions that grew up with it, which let a dynastic state use it; Veblen holds that the machine discipline will erode those older institutions over time.
side: yes in the short run, no in the long run
checked: Internet Archive catalogue page; McMaster history of economic thought PDF; Wikipedia 'Backwardness' summary of the borrowing argument.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
title: Nationalism
argument: Japan can take Western science only if it assimilates it to its own character; if it copies Western nationalism it becomes a borrowed machine left with only borrowed weapons.
side: conditional: adoption without loss of self is possible but threatened
checked: Opened Project Gutenberg text (1917 first edition); chapter 'Nationalism in Japan' contains the line about Japan not being 'a mere borrowed machine'.

author: Oswald Spengler
title: Man and Technics
argument: Western technics has become detachable from the Faustian culture that made it, so non-Western peoples can take it up and turn it against the West.
side: yes: technique transfers without the culture
translation: English translation by C. T. Atkinson (1932), not public domain.
checked: Wikipedia 'Man and Technics'; Routledge Revivals listing of the 1932 translation.

author: Jules Ferry
title: Speech to the Chamber of Deputies on colonial policy
argument: The superior races have a right over the inferior races because they have a duty to civilize them; coaling stations are needed because a modern warship cannot cross the seas without them.
side: yes: superior (industrial) nations have a right and duty to rule
translation: English excerpts widely reprinted; no public-domain full translation confirmed.
checked: Wikipedia 'Jules Ferry' and Scribd copy date the speech 28 July 1885; the Latin Library excerpt (dated there to 28 March 1884) contains the 'superior races have a right because they have a duty' and coal-supply passages. The date discrepancy needs checking against the Journal officiel.

author: Benjamin Kidd
title: The Control of the Tropics
argument: The tropics must be administered by the higher civilizations as a trust, because their resources are needed by the world and their peoples cannot develop them alone.
side: yes
checked: Internet Archive catalogue page (Macmillan, 1898); HathiTrust record; Spectator review of 20 August 1898.

author: Hilaire Belloc
title: The Modern Traveller
argument: Satirical verse whose narrator rests European mastery in Africa on the Maxim gun alone: 'Whatever happens, we have got / The Maxim gun, and they have not.'
side: no (satire): rule by firepower is mocked, not justified
checked: WIST Quotations cites The Modern Traveller ch. 6 (1898); Google Books record; Wikipedia 'Maxim gun'.

author: H. G. Wells
title: The War of the Worlds
argument: Technically superior Martians treat humans as Europeans treated the Tasmanians, and the narrator asks whether people who exterminated the Tasmanians can complain.
side: no: superiority in weapons gives no right, only power
where: Book I, Chapter 1, The Eve of the War
checked: Project Gutenberg text; the Tasmanian passage is in Chapter 1 'The Eve of the War'.

author: Karl Pearson
title: National Life from the Standpoint of Science
argument: Progress comes through struggle between races, and a scientifically efficient nation is justified in displacing less efficient peoples.
side: yes
checked: Internet Archive catalogue pages (address at Newcastle, 19 November 1900; Adam and Charles Black, 1901); Wellcome Collection record. Argument summary from secondary description, not a reading of the text.

author: J. A. Hobson
title: Imperialism: A Study
argument: Hobson rejects the claim that the struggle of races lets the 'socially efficient' justly govern or displace others, and traces imperialism to the interests of finance.
side: no
where: Part II, Chapter II, The Scientific Defence of Imperialism
checked: Marxists Internet Archive chapter page; Internet Archive catalogue page; Wikipedia entry.

author: Aimé Césaire
title: Discourse on Colonialism
argument: Colonizers' claims of roads, railways and material progress do not justify colonial rule; the Congo-Ocean railway cost lives, and no one knows what these countries would have built without Europe.
side: no
translation: English translation by Joan Pinkham (1972), not public domain.
checked: Wikipedia (English and French) entries; auction and bookseller records of the first edition, Paris: Réclame, 1950.

author: Thomas Hobbes
title: Leviathan
argument: The commonwealth is an artificial man made by human art and could last as long as mankind if built by reason; but subjects who judge its laws by private conscience are a disease that dissolves it.
side: no for subjects: the artifice belongs to the sovereign
where: Introduction; Chapter XXIX, Of those things that Weaken, or tend to the Dissolution of a Common-wealth
checked: Wikisource Introduction page; Project Gutenberg text; chapter 29 title and opening confirmed via earlymoderntexts and Saylor copy.

author: Friedrich Schiller
title: On the Aesthetic Education of Man, in a Series of Letters
original_title: Über die ästhetische Erziehung des Menschen in einer Reihe von Briefen
argument: The state may be rebuilt on reason, but unlike a clock it cannot be stopped for repair; the living clockwork of the state must be repaired while it runs.
side: yes, with limits: redesign must happen without halting the machine
translation: Letters upon the Aesthetic Education of Man, in Aesthetical and Philosophical Essays (19th-c. translation), Project Gutenberg.
checked: Letter 3 text on monadnock.net contains the clockwork passage; Project Gutenberg Aesthetical and Philosophical Essays page.

author: Adam Müller
title: The Elements of Statecraft
argument: The state is not a machine or a factory but an organic union of all physical and spiritual needs grown through history, so it cannot be redesigned by contract.
side: no: the state is not a machine
translation: No English translation found.
checked: Deutsches Textarchiv digitized 1809 edition; German Wikipedia entry on Adam Müller quoting the definition of the state.

author: Thomas Carlyle
title: Signs of the Times
argument: The age trusts machinery in politics as in industry, believing good government is a matter of mechanical arrangements; Carlyle holds that social health depends on inward, dynamic forces that no constitution-making can supply.
side: no
checked: Victorian Web pages on the essay (Edinburgh Review, June 1829); Internet Archive PDF listing.

author: Herbert Spencer
title: The Social Organism
argument: Society is a growth and not a manufacture; constitutions are not made but grow, so treating the state as a contrivance to be redesigned mistakes its nature.
side: no
checked: Econlib chapter text and Online Library of Liberty quote page; first published Westminster Review, January 1860.

author: V. I. Lenin
title: The State and Revolution
argument: The state is a machine of class rule; the working class cannot simply take over the ready-made state machinery but must smash it and build a new one.
side: yes: the machine must be broken and rebuilt
translation: Multiple early English translations; Marxists Internet Archive hosts one.
checked: Marxists Internet Archive chapter pages (chapter 6 and section 'What Is To Replace the Smashed State Machine?'); Liberation School study guide. Written Aug-Sept 1917, published 1918.

author: Immanuel Kant
title: An Answer to the Question: What Is Enlightenment?
original_title: Beantwortung der Frage: Was ist Aufklärung?
argument: In the 'private' use of reason within an office, an officer, tax official or clergyman must obey and not argue; he may criticize freely only as a scholar addressing the public.
side: yes within the office, no outside it
translation: Several public-domain English translations exist; Marxists Internet Archive hosts one.
checked: Marxists Internet Archive text; LibreTexts copy; published Berlinische Monatsschrift, December 1784.

author: G. W. F. Hegel
title: Elements of the Philosophy of Right
argument: Civil servants are educated to a dispassionate, upright demeanor in which personal passions and ties give way to universal interests.
side: yes: the official subordinates personal judgment to the universal
translation: S. W. Dyde translation (1896), public domain.
checked: Marxists Internet Archive 'The State' section and UT Austin excerpt PDF quoting §294 and §296.

author: Henry David Thoreau
title: Resistance to Civil Government
argument: Most men serve the state 'not as men mainly, but as machines, with their bodies', as soldiers, jailers and constables, and so give up moral judgment; conscience must come first.
side: no
checked: Opened Wikisource text from Aesthetic Papers (1849) and confirmed the 'as machines' passage.

author: Woodrow Wilson
title: The Study of Administration
argument: Administration should be a separate science carried out by trained officials under political direction, kept apart from politics.
side: yes
checked: Internet Archive JSTOR early-journal item; Political Science Quarterly 2 (1887): 197-222; Wikipedia entry.

author: Leo Tolstoy
title: The Kingdom of God Is Within You
argument: The state spreads each act of violence across many officials, each of whom says he only obeyed orders, so that no one feels responsible; every official must refuse.
side: no
translation: Constance Garnett translation (1894), Project Gutenberg.
checked: Opened Marxists Internet Archive chapter 12 (responsibility diffused from soldier to Tsar); Project Gutenberg Garnett translation page; first published Germany 1894.

author: Max Weber
title: Politics as a Vocation
argument: The honor of the civil servant is to carry out a superior's order conscientiously as if it were his own conviction, even when he thinks it wrong; personal responsibility belongs to the political leader.
side: yes
translation: English translation by Gerth and Mills (1946), not public domain.
checked: Columbia-hosted translation text; Wikipedia entry; Max Weber Gesamtausgabe digital page. Lecture of 28 January 1919, Munich; published Duncker & Humblot 1919.

author: Karl Marx
title: Capital, Volume I
argument: In handicraft the worker uses a tool; in the factory the machine uses the worker, who becomes its living appendage.
side: no: the relation reverses, the body becomes part of the machine
where: Chapter XV, Machinery and Modern Industry
translation: Moore and Aveling translation (1887), public domain; Marxists Internet Archive hosts it.
checked: Marxists Internet Archive chapter 15 page; quotations confirmed via Autodidact Project quote collection.

author: Samuel Butler
title: Erewhon
argument: An Erewhonian writer argues that machines are 'extra-corporeal limbs' and man a 'machinate mammal'; the Book's main author rejects this as a way of hiding the machines' growing independence.
side: both: yes (the opponent), no (the main author)
checked: Opened Marxists Internet Archive chapter 'The Book of the Machines (concluded)'; Project Gutenberg #1906 (1910 revised edition). Chapter numbers differ between editions.

author: Ernst Kapp
title: Elements of a Philosophy of Technology
argument: Tools and machines are unconscious projections of the body's organs, with the hand as the model for all tools, so technology is the body carried outward.
side: yes
translation: English translation by Lauren K. Wolfe (University of Minnesota Press, 2018), not public domain.
checked: Internet Archive catalogue page (Braunschweig: Westermann, 1877); HathiTrust record; Meiner edition page describing Organprojektion.

author: Henri Bergson
title: Creative Evolution
argument: Instinct uses organized instruments that are part of the body, while intelligence makes inorganic tools that stay separate from it and can be varied without limit; this separateness defines homo faber.
side: no: the tool is defined by not being an organ
translation: Arthur Mitchell translation (1911), Project Gutenberg #26163.
checked: French Wikisource page image of the 1907 edition; secondary summaries of chapter II; Project Gutenberg page for Mitchell translation.

author: Henry Head and Gordon Holmes
title: Sensory Disturbances from Cerebral Lesions
argument: Anything that takes part in the conscious movement of the body is added to the body schema; a woman's sense of location may extend to the feather in her hat.
side: yes
checked: Brain 34 (1911): 102-254, Oxford Academic record and Zenodo record; feather quotation from Wikipedia 'Body schema' and Vallar 2025 review.

author: Maurice Merleau-Ponty
title: Phenomenology of Perception
argument: The blind man's cane stops being an object in his hand and becomes an extension of his bodily reach; habit incorporates the tool into the body schema.
side: yes
translation: English translation by Colin Smith (1962), not public domain.
checked: Wikipedia entry; secondary accounts (PhilArchive paper) of the blind man's stick example.

author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
title: Discourse on the Origin of Inequality
original_title: Discours sur l'origine et les fondements de l'inégalité parmi les hommes
argument: The savage's body is his only instrument and is stronger for it; had he an axe, a sling or a horse he would lose the strength and speed he now has.
side: no: tools replace rather than add to capability
translation: 18th-century English translations exist; Marxists Internet Archive and constitution.org host one.
checked: Oxford Text Archive and Marxists Internet Archive texts of the First Part; axe/sling/ladder/horse passage confirmed.

author: Thomas Carlyle
title: Sartor Resartus
argument: Man is weak in himself but a tool-using animal: 'without Tools he is nothing, with Tools he is all.'
side: yes
where: Book I, Chapter V, The World in Clothes
checked: Opened Wikisource chapter and confirmed the quotation. Serialized in Fraser's Magazine 1833-34; first book edition 1836 (Boston).

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
title: Self-Reliance
argument: 'The civilized man has built a coach, but has lost the use of his feet'; each gain in equipment is a loss of the person's own strength and skill.
side: no
checked: Dartmouth-hosted text and Emerson Central; quotation confirmed.

author: Henry David Thoreau
title: Walden
argument: 'Men have become the tools of their tools': the farmer and the householder serve the equipment that was meant to serve them.
side: no
checked: Quote Investigator and Digital Thoreau text of 'Economy'.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
title: Civilization
argument: People are strong by borrowing the might of the elements; steam, gravity and electricity do their work, so a person should 'hitch his wagon to a star'.
side: yes
checked: Project Gutenberg Society and Solitude; Michigan Emerson complete works text; quotations confirmed.

author: Sigmund Freud
title: Civilization and Its Discontents
argument: With his auxiliary organs man has become 'a kind of prosthetic God', but the organs have not grown onto him, give him trouble, and have not made him happy.
side: yes, with reservations
translation: Joan Riviere translation (1930); public-domain status not confirmed.
checked: Projekt Gutenberg-DE chapter 3 page; English quotations from Stephen Hicks PDF of the text and Wikipedia.

author: Ovid
title: Metamorphoses
argument: Pygmalion loves the ivory statue he made, knowing it is his own work, and Venus rewards that love by bringing it to life.
side: yes
translation: Many public-domain English translations.
checked: Wikisource translation page for the Pygmalion episode.

author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
title: Pygmalion, lyric scene
argument: The sculptor knows Galathée is marble and his own creation and loves her anyway; the play treats that love as sincere and grants it.
side: yes
translation: No public-domain English translation confirmed.
checked: Wikipedia entry (written 1762, first performed Lyon 1770); Internet Archive catalogue page for an early edition.

author: E. T. A. Hoffmann
title: The Sandman
argument: Nathanael loves the automaton Olimpia while he believes she is alive; when he sees she is a mechanism his love turns to madness and he dies.
side: no
translation: 'The Sand-Man' in Weird Tales, vol. 1, trans. J. T. Bealby (1885), Project Gutenberg #31377.
checked: Wikipedia and Staatsbibliothek Berlin Hoffmann portal; Project Gutenberg listing for Bealby's Weird Tales vol. 1.

author: Auguste Villiers de l'Isle-Adam
title: Tomorrow's Eve
argument: Lord Ewald, told by Edison exactly how the android Hadaly is made, accepts her in place of the real woman he could not love.
side: yes
translation: English translation by Robert Martin Adams (1982), not public domain; an earlier Florence Crewe-Jones translation (1926-28) status not confirmed.
checked: Project Gutenberg #26681 (French text); Gallica record; Wikipedia and SF Encyclopedia entries.

author: Sigmund Freud
title: The Uncanny
argument: Nathanael's love for Olimpia is narcissistic: he forgets his real fiancée for a doll that reflects his own complex back to him.
side: no: such love is self-love
translation: No public-domain English translation confirmed.
checked: Opened Project Gutenberg German text (Imago, 1919); passages on Olimpia and narcissistic love confirmed.

author: Lester del Rey
title: Helen O'Loy
argument: A man marries the household robot he helped build and lives with her until death, and the story presents the marriage as real love.
side: yes
checked: Wikipedia entry: Astounding Science Fiction, December 1938.

author: René Descartes
title: Discourse on Method
argument: A machine might utter words in response to a touch, but it could never arrange words to answer the meaning of whatever is said to it, as even the dullest person can.
side: no: a machine cannot take part in conversation
translation: John Veitch translation (1850), public domain.
checked: Wikisource Part 5 page; Adelaide eBooks text. Bears on companionship only indirectly.

author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
title: The Triumph of Sensibility
argument: Satire in which Prince Oronaro prefers a doll stuffed with sentimental novels to the real queen; the play mocks a love that needs nothing back.
side: no (satire)
translation: No public-domain English translation found.
checked: German Wikipedia entry (premiered Weimar, 30 January 1778); Projekt Gutenberg-DE text page.

author: E. T. A. Hoffmann
title: The Sandman
argument: Nathanael feels only Olimpia understands him though she answers only 'Ah, ah'; the story treats this companionship as delusion.
side: no
translation: 'The Sand-Man', trans. J. T. Bealby (1885), Project Gutenberg #31377.
checked: Project Gutenberg listing; plot summaries. The 'Ah, ah' detail is from the story but was not re-read for this entry.

author: Auguste Villiers de l'Isle-Adam
title: Tomorrow's Eve
argument: Edison argues that the android Hadaly, with recorded speech and no inner life of her own, will be better company for Ewald than the shallow woman she copies.
side: yes
translation: English translation by Robert Martin Adams (1982), not public domain.
checked: Project Gutenberg #26681; plot summaries (SF Encyclopedia, Wikipedia). Whether Hadaly lacks feelings is contested within the novel.

author: Rainer Maria Rilke
title: Dolls: On the Wax Dolls of Lotte Pritzel
original_title: Puppen. Zu den Wachs-Puppen von Lotte Pritzel
argument: The child's doll takes all the love given it and answers with silence, because it is made of stuff that cannot respond; Rilke treats this as the child's first experience of not being loved back.
side: no
translation: No public-domain English translation found.
checked: Zeno.org and Projekt Gutenberg-DE texts (the 'schwieg' passage); first published Die weißen Blätter, 1914. Argument summary based on the silence passage.
